entries.title: €561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink
entries.summary: The budget for 2027 has reached new highs, and pension funds, defense spending and a weak economy are increasing the pressure. At the same time, tensions are mounting within the government.

entries.title: US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
entries.summary: The US Army says a controlled blast is the safest way to deal with explosive chemicals that began crystallizing in storage. US President Donald Trump said "mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations."
entries.content:
United States of America

US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa

November 25, 2026

The US Army says a controlled blast is the safest way to deal with explosive chemicals that began crystallizing in storage. US President Donald Trump said "mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations."

The United States Army detonated nearly 5 tons of aging lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday, saying the explosive chemical has become too unstable to store.

The controlled blast occurred a little after 9 a.m. local time (1500 GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and will destroy the country's entire stockpile of the chemical. Plumes of smoke were seen on camera in video footage after the controlled blast in Middletown.

The US Army has said residents of a small town and other nearby areas should leave "out of an abundance of caution."

"We don't believe that the public should be in a panic," said acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."

"Early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

What do we know?

The material was moved to Iowa for storage from bases around the country in 2009.

But a March inspection found that it had partly crystallized, which makes it sensitive to friction and cold and could set off a spontaneous explosion.

"Inaction is no longer an option," said Major General Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.

Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, told reporters: "It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."

Is it safe to detonate the chemical?

To limit toxic lead dust, the Army has built barriers around the bunkers holding the material and will use foam and water to trap particles.

Reuters reported that Army projections show dust could settle up to 40 miles (64 km) southwest, reaching northern Missouri.

Officials expect the wind to carry the plume away from Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people.

While residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) were encouraged to evacuate, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has also advised people 5 to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.

How have people reacted?

The date of the detonation changed three times after public backlash over its impact on the environment and public health. A federal appeals court cleared the plan on Monday after environmental groups sued.

Farmer Jill Holler, who organized a protest, told Reuters: "I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option."

"What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying," she added.

entries.title: EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules
entries.summary: European General Court ruled that the European Commission has failed to set out a timeline after pledging to end caged farming by the end of 2023.
entries.content:
November 25, 2026

European General Court ruled that the European Commission has failed to set out a timeline after pledging to end caged farming by the end of 2023.

A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a new timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.

Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.

In 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages. The move came after 1,4 million people signed a petition.

But it failed to follow up on the pledge. This resulted in the campaigners requesting a new timeline and eventually led to a court case when that was also not happening.

The Luxembourg-based General Court, the European Union's second-highest, on Wednesday ruled in favor of the animal rights campaigners.

"The Commission is under an obligation — which is not limited in time — to set out a timeline for all the measures which it intends to take in response to such an initiative," the court said.

According to the "European citizens' initiative" system, the Commission has to receive the petitions that gather over one million signatures across at least seven bloc countries. However, it is not obligated to meet the demands.

The court noted that if the Commission decides to take action, it has to keep the public and the European Parliament posted on a timeline in accordance with the principle of "good administration."

About 143 million chickens are kept in cages in EU

The Commission said it was analyzing the ruling before making a decision. It can still appeal the ruling.

It has previously stated an intention to put forward a proposal for the phased elimination of cage systems for chickens by the end of this year, as well as a separate proposal to transition from farrowing crates to pen-based systems for pigs by 2027.

According to the Albert Schweitzer Foundation, no timetable has been set for calves, rabbits, ducks, geese and quail.

In the EU, about 143 million egg-laying chickens are kept in cages while the majority of female pigs spend at least part of their lives caged.

The use of cage systems in agricultural production accredited as "organic" is already prohibited in the EU.

entries.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
entries.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

November 25, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

entries.title: Ukraine: Poland to set up no-fly zone near Ukraine border
entries.summary: Poland urged NATO allies to be vigilant at their borders after repeated Russian airspace incursions. Allies have also offered different opinions on Kyiv attacking Russian ships in Libya. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Poland to create no-fly zone near Ukraine border

Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026

Poland urged NATO allies to be vigilant at their borders after repeated Russian airspace incursions. Allies have also offered different opinions on Kyiv attacking Russian ships in Libya. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Poland hopes to establish a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine by the end of the year
  • Russia attacks have halted output at Ukrainian gas facilities as well as a thermal power plant
  • Ukraine says it attacked Russian oil facilities in the Samara region
  • France's foreign minister defended Ukraine's attacks on Russian shadow fleet ships off the Libyan coast, though Italy's called the attack 'a mistake'
  • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned against ending Ukraine support, saying 'Russia wants more than Ukraine'

Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:

Skip next section Russian sources say Europeans must take up Putin's offer for Moscow talks

Russian sources say Europeans must take up Putin's offer for Moscow talks

Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.

Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained."

Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations."

He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.

Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are."

Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve."

Skip next section Poland to create no-fly zone at Ukraine border, urges others to do same

Poland to create no-fly zone at Ukraine border, urges others to do same

Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that Warsaw will set up a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and suggested other regional allies do the same in the wake of repeated Russian incursions into NATO airspace as part of Moscow's war of aggression.

"An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk.

"We will also urge our allies — the ⁠entire ​NATO alliance — to establish such a ​principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer ​in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead."

Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already.

On Wednesday, Tomczyk said the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces.

Skip next section Merz defends Ukraine aid, says those opposed are lost or have other aims

Merz defends Ukraine aid, says those opposed are lost or have other aims

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate in the Bundestag on Wednesday.

Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly ​what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine." 

"Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia ​is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added.

Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims."

The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow.

Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO.

Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself.

"We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense ⁠technology."

Skip next section Moscow, Kyiv exchange overnight attacks on energy infrastructure

Moscow, Kyiv exchange overnight attacks on energy infrastructure

Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in.

Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.

Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.

In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.

Skip next section France, Italy offer different takes on Ukraine's actions in Libya

France, Italy offer different takes on Ukraine's actions in Libya

Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the issue.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.

Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity."

Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?"

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.

Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on ⁠Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in ​Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port."

Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.

Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.

While Moscow chided former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson's calls for a contingent of Western soldiers to be stationed in Ukraine, France's foreign minister defended Kyiv's recent attacks on Russian maritime vessels in far away Libya — something Italy's foreign minister criticized.

In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended German support for Ukraine as opposition parties with sympathies for Moscow complain it's too expensive.

Merz called out those wanting to curtail support as either "failing to grasp" the fact that "Russia wants more than Ukraine" or "pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism."

Lastly, Poland's defense minister on Wednesday expressed astonishment over the fact that the US has not yet condemned or even reacted to repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace in recent days.

Stay tuned to DW for these stories and all the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine….

entries.title: US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 others
entries.summary: The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high living costs.
entries.content:
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026

The Trump administration is planning new import duties of up to 20% to counter excessive manufacturing abroad. The measures could put further pressure on US consumers already struggling with high living costs.

The United States on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled the proposed duties after completing an eight-month investigation into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.

Washington accuses the targeted economies of promoting excessive industrial production, allowing cheaper goods to undercut American manufacturers.

The proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Wednesday. However, he added that some rates could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.

The duties will be subject to a public comment period and a hearing before taking effect, possibly in January at the earliest.

Which countries would face new US tariffs?

China would face an additional tariff of 20%, the joint-highest rate among the targeted economies.

The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as the 19% cap agreed with Malaysia, a senior US administration official said.

Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam would also be affected.

Mexico and Norway are currently excluded from the proposed measures. Greer said talks with Mexico were continuing as Washington's investigation into its trade practices remained ongoing.

In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed higher tariffs on Brazilian raw and refined sugar and a new 10% duty on aircraft, which would affect Brazilian manufacturer Embraer.

How would the new US tariffs work?

The senior US official said the proposed duties would not exceed tariff limits negotiated under existing trade agreements.

However, the new tariffs on China would be added to duties of around 25% imposed during Trump's first term, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%.

Around $30 billion worth of Chinese imports that Washington is considering for tariff reductions would be exempt from the new measures.

The proposed duties would not be added to existing sector-specific tariffs on products such as automobiles, steel and aluminum.

Nor would they be combined with tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% imposed in July against 60 trading partners over alleged insufficient action against forced labor. Where both measures apply, the higher rate would prevail.

How have the EU and China responded to the US tariffs?

The European Union said on Wednesday it would examine the proposed US tariffs but rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production.

"We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity," the EU said, adding that it expected Washington to honor the trade agreement reached with Brussels last year.

Beijing also rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production and reiterated its opposition to trade wars, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Washington has accused Beijing of flooding global markets with cheap exports, ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.

Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping last week in Shenzhen and is due to host him at the G20 summit in Miami in December.

An existing trade truce between Washington and Beijing is set to expire on January 10. Access to rare earth minerals and Chinese purchases of US agricultural products could feature in further negotiations.

Why is Trump introducing new tariffs?

The measures are intended in part to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.

The court ruled that Trump lacked the authority to impose the duties by declaring an economic emergency and bypassing Congress.

The new measures instead rely on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and retaliate against unfair or discriminatory foreign trade practices.

Trump has repeatedly promised that tariffs will bring manufacturing jobs back to the US and reduce the federal deficit.

Could Trump's new tariffs fuel US inflation?

The proposed duties could put further pressure on American businesses, which may pass additional costs on to consumers.

US consumer inflation reached 3.7% year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high. Earlier tariffs, the effects of Trump's war on Iran and a boom in artificial intelligence investment have contributed to rising prices.

High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party lose control of both chambers of Congress.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the elections found that 62% of respondents supported efforts to repeal Trump's tariffs.

entries.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
entries.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing.
entries.content:
November 25, 2026

German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing.

"Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future."

That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time.

German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China. 

"For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steimeier said during the event.

"One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us."

Why Africa matters?

Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next decades, emerging as a key source of future labor.

Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home.

Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics.

The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential, is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains.

It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia.

German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia.

"We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).

"It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW.

What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy?

Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure.

African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business.

Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent.

German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries.

However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades.

Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies.

Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk.

"German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there."

The 2026 World Investment Report by UN trade body UNCTAD showed that investors from the Gulf and Asia are becoming important sources of investment in Africa, especially in energy, logistics, real estate and infrastructure.

The UAE has been a major investor in greenfield megaprojects in recent years, including the $34 billion (€31 billion) Infinity Power renewable energy project in Mauritania, the $24 billion Ras El Hikma real estate development project in Egypt and the $6 billion H2 Global Energy hydrogen project in Tunisia.

How can German firms seize the African opportunity?

Business leaders are calling for better financing and guarantees and more risk-sharing and easing of bureaucratic hurdles.

Meanwhile, others, including the German president, are urging German businesses to take on more risk and seize opportunities in Africa. Otherwise, they risk being edged out by foreign rivals.

"Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future," Steinmeier said.

entries.title: Ice hockey prospect Max Calce follows Leon Draisaitl's path, leaving Mannheim for Canada
entries.summary: The player widely seen as Germany's biggest ice hockey talent to come along in years is leaving the country's top professional league for Canada – changing tracks in his bid to make it to the NHL.
entries.content:
November 25, 2026

The player widely seen as Germany's biggest ice hockey talent to come along in years is leaving the country's top professional league for Canada – changing tracks in his bid to make it to the NHL.

Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.

"I have long had three goals," he said. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home."

Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.

The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.

This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.

Mature decision-making on the ice

"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," said former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.

"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision."

Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.

In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.

"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person."

This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.

"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director said.

"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition."

Increased visibility ahead of NHL draft

On the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.

In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.

This, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.

Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

entries.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
entries.summary: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?
entries.content:
India

Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine

November 25, 2026

Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?

Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.

But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.

After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.

In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.

Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India.

He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.

India's efforts to bring recruits home

The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.

At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.

In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.

The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.

The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.

Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.

Duped or desperate?

Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.

"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.

He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.

"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.

The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.

Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine. 

He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.

"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.

Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.

Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.

"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.

He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.

Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy

India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.

The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.

Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.

He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.

"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.

Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.

"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.
